OSLO/KYIV/WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday after what a US official called "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Norway, as President Donald Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war.

The US official said Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which also involved the leaders of Norway and Finland and European and NATO representatives, and that participants made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia.

The official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture.

Witkoff would aim to "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," the official said.

Zelenskiy travelled to Oslo seeking to repair relations with Washington, which have sunk to new lows as Trump has courted Moscow. Kyiv has complained that Washington has withheld vital military support and intelligence.

Zelenskiy told a news conference after the Oslo meeting and an earlier phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Ukraine was again receiving early warnings of Russian missile attacks.

"Now it works, it's great," he said, adding he and Rubio had discussed supplies of Patriot missile interceptors as well as the satellite-based Starlink system, which Kyiv complained had stopped working when mounted on fast-moving objects such as drones.

Trump's recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals.

Zelenskiy said he had discussed "Article 5-like" security guarantees, referring to the NATO stipulation that an attack on one ally is an attack on all.

"I am thankful to the American side that they underlined again that it will be strong," he said.

Zelenskiy reiterated that Ukraine hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting of leaders of Ukraine, Russia and the US.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere told the news conference the Oslo meeting had been good and constructive, while Finnish President Alexander Stubb added: "I think the (peace) process is back on track."

Washington has denied deliberately hindering Ukraine's war effort. But Trump has repeatedly rebuked Zelenskiy, and called for him to be replaced.

On Tuesday, Trump called on Ukraine to make a deal to settle the war, and said Moscow wanted to get it done. "Ukraine has to want to settle this war," he told reporters.

Trump suggested Moscow had the upper hand in the fight because "Russia is a big machine — they just keep grinding forward, and that's what they've done. They've taken a very large piece of land."

RUBIO SAYS US MISSILES MAY NOT HAVE BEEN DELIVERED YET

The US under Trump has largely stopped providing weapons directly to Ukraine but lets European countries buy US weaponry on Kyiv's behalf under a program known as Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL). It has also provided intelligence and technology that Europe cannot match.

A source familiar with the matter said most weapons deliveries under PURL continued to flow, but US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had not approved Ukraine’s latest requests for Patriot interceptors.

Rubio acknowledged on Tuesday that a consignment of interceptors bought by European countries for Ukraine may not have been delivered, but denied that the US had changed policy.

"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said on a visit to India.

Hegseth told reporters US policy toward Ukraine had not changed and stressed the need to maintain US stockpiles. "Certainly, with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well," he said.

He also said Washington had not pulled back Ukraine's ability to access Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and appeared to signal that the problem rested with corporate terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with.

Musk has said Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink communications system, is controlled by the US government and any limits on its use are ultimately up to Trump.

Tuesday's Wall Street Journal cited US officials and people familiar with the matter as saying that Musk ordered the slowdown after consulting with Trump and other administration officials. Reuters reported earlier that the order to limit the service came from the White House.

While US ties with Ukraine have deteriorated, Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukrainian cities, particularly targeting power stations and fuel, despite a call from Trump for both sides to spare each other's energy systems.

Russia bombarded cities in western Ukraine overnight, targeting electricity systems and knocking out power across swathes of the country that had previously been spared.

Ukraine held back for several days last week from hitting Russian oil refineries in deference to Trump's request, but has resumed strikes after Russia showed no sign of complying. Both sides have also struck data centres.

Trump has repeatedly condemned Ukrainian attacks on Russia while saying little about Russia's far more severe attacks on Ukraine.

RUSSIAN ATTACKS

Russia's defence ministry said on Tuesday it struck three cargo vessels in Ukraine's port of Reni and two other cargo vessels en route to Odesa. Russian forces also hit two logistics hubs, it said.

Energy facilities were attacked in seven Ukrainian regions overnight, knocking out power, and the western Lviv region was struck again during the day. Russian drones also struck an energy facility in Kyiv on Tuesday, mayor Vitali Klitschko said, with authorities saying power was out in four districts.

The deterioration of US-Ukraine relations began 10 days ago when Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel in a deal agreed with Putin. Trump said this would help reduce high fuel prices that have upset US voters ahead of midterm elections on November 3.

At the weekend, Trump issued a broad waiver of tougher sanctions on Russia that were meant to have begun this week.

items.title: Iran prolongs talks in stalemate to influence US midterms, officials say
items.content_html:
DUBAI, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Iran has deliberately prolonged talks with the US to try to weaken Donald Trump politically ahead of November's US midterm elections, senior officials say, while fears of renewed military action and deep distrust of Washington have reinforced Tehran's reluctance to strike a quick deal to end the war.

Three senior Iranian officials and an Iranian insider, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Tehran was convinced the US president was ready to resort to renewed attacks to try to break the stalemate in the eight-month-old war.

"Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," one of the officials said. "The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory."

Tehran analyst Saeed Leylaz said that, by prolonging the talks, "Iran is influencing the US election without taking any unlawful action".

IRAN CAN EXPLOIT TRUMP'S POLITICAL PROBLEMS

The war, which began in February when the US and its ally Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump’s approval rating to a record low as polls suggest that Americans worried about high gasoline prices will punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections.

Trump has repeatedly said he expects oil prices to drop after the elections, but has not offered a detailed plan to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route effectively closed by Iran since the war began.

Iranian attacks both threatened and real have kept ship traffic through the strait to a trickle, while a US maritime blockade and trade sanctions have cut off Iran's oil export revenues and exacerbated growing domestic economic woes.

With Tehran refusing to make concessions it believes could benefit Trump politically, there is little chance of a breakthrough before the elections, the officials said.

Under pressure from Israel, Washington wants Iran’s decades-long nuclear programme - which Iran says is purely peaceful and Western powers allege has military dimensions - on the table from the outset.

For its part, Tehran insists that its conditions under a "seven-day plan" must be met before nuclear negotiations begin. And it offers no prospect of giving up the leverage over the Strait of Hormuz that the conflict prompted it to seize.

Iran's Foreign Ministry and the US White House did not respond to Reuters requests for comment.

IRAN CANNOT TRUST WASHINGTON, OFFICIALS SAY

Iran’s proposal, conveyed through Qatari mediators, offered to reopen the strait within seven days, albeit under Iranian control, provided that Washington lifted its maritime blockade, eased restrictions on Iranian oil exports, released frozen assets and ended hostilities on all fronts.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the offer remained on the table, with messages being exchanged through mediators.

Tehran's view that Washington cannot be trusted to commit to diplomacy stems from the attacks on Iran that have derailed previous negotiations, one Iranian official said.

In June 2025, an Israeli attack wrecked plans for a sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks in Oman. And last February, the US and Israel launched their war just after another round of talks ended, with further technical discussions scheduled.

Maintaining a state somewhere between war and peace through the US midterms allows Iran to sustain pressure on Washington while reiterating its commitment to diplomacy.

Trump has said the US will not bomb Iran again before November 3. However, the officials said Tehran continues to expect that bombing will resume, sooner or later.

Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said the clerical establishment clearly wanted to hurt Trump politically.

"But the fundamental issue is that Tehran believes that Trump is interested in regime change ... and following Israeli Prime Minister (Benjamin) Netanyahu’s policy of seeking to bring down Iran’s ruling establishment," he said.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Netanyahu on Monday, three Israeli officials said, in an unannounced visit to Israel a week before a parliamentary election in which Netanyahu's position is at risk.

RETURN TO PREWAR STATUS IMPOSSIBLE FOR IRAN, SAYS ANALYST

Iran’s strategy of keeping negotiations alive without rushing towards agreement comes at a cost.

Prolonged uncertainty is weighing on Iran’s already crippled economy and wearing down public patience. Thousands were killed at the turn of the year when the security forces crushed spiralling anti-government protests.

Annual inflation hit 73.6% in September, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran, and the rial currency has fallen nearly 35% against the dollar since Washington reapplied its naval blockade in July.

Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5, according to energy intelligence platform Vortexa.

But the leadership's distrust of Washington extends beyond the current conflict to existential concerns. Iran believes the US has repeatedly broken agreements even when Tehran honoured its commitments, Leylaz said, leaving little confidence that any comprehensive deal would endure.

“Reaching a sustainable deal with the US, even after the Trump administration, is no longer possible because of the deepened distrust,” Leylaz said. "Nothing will go back to the pre-war status quo."

items.title: Could disillusioned Kansas voters send their first Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years?
items.content_html:
GARDEN CITY, Kansas, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The last time the state of Kansas sent a Democrat to the US Senate, the Great Depression was ravaging the state, wheat prices had collapsed and drought was turning the Great Plains into the Dust Bowl.

Some 94 years later, Kansas may do it again.

Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, is running neck and neck with Republican US Senator Roger Marshall, based on both a New York Times/Siena Poll, opens new tab and Emerson College Polling, opens new tab, in a state that Republican President Donald Trump won in 2024 with more than 57% of the vote.

The unexpectedly competitive race reflects strains in the Republican heartland, where Democrats are betting that soaring farm costs, including near-record-high diesel, and discontent with Trump's immigration crackdown can revive the region's progressive populist tradition.

In the converted grain bin that serves as an office for Vance and Louise Ehmke's wheat farm and seed business, John Brown, the abolitionist who took up arms against slavery in Kansas, stares down from a reproduction of a famous painting.

In 1885, 20 years after the Civil War, Vance Ehmke’s ancestors started farming in western Kansas. But now, climbing costs linked to the US-Israeli war on Iran have him contemplating a dark future for his farm and others around it.

“During the past year, we have seen fuel prices just darn near double,” Ehmke said. “That’s cost us $50,000 of unexpected expenses.”

COST OF FUEL, FERTILIZER

Fuel and fertilizer prices have shot up dramatically since the war started in February, with diesel used to power farm equipment up 70% since the war began.

Those rising costs have reverberated in states like Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska, where agriculture dominates local economies.

In Iowa, opinion polls show Republican US Representative Ashley Hinson in a tight Senate race with Democrat Josh Turek for the seat being vacated by Republican Joni Ernst.

Hinson called last month for an "immediate end" to the Iran war in a social media post that said Iowans "shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war."

In Nebraska, Republican Senator Pete Ricketts faces a competitive race against independent Dan Osborn, despite Trump winning the state by more than 20 points in 2024.

Democrats need to pick up four US Senate seats to win control of the chamber.

TRUMP, JD VANCE STUMP FOR AT-RISK REPUBLICANS

Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other leading Republicans have stumped for at-risk candidates in the Midwest region.

Trump pledged in Nebraska this month to expand access to tax-exempt diesel fuel and, in a Wichita-area rally on Monday, said the US Department of Agriculture would launch a "harvest fuel relief program" to provide farmers with $8 billion to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

Hamilton still has an uphill climb with many rural Kansas voters. Not far from the Ehmkes is another farm owned by Ron Suppes, a Republican who supports Marshall.

“We’ve had high diesel prices in prior years. I don’t know if it matters which administration,” he said.

“I’ll put up with the pain for a while."

Another Trump priority hit the Kansas meatpacking industry in late September, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrested 104 people in Dodge City, Garden City, Liberal and surrounding areas, according to the US Attorney's Office for the District of Kansas.

Amid voter anger over high beef prices, the raids slowed operations at major processors including Cargill and National Beef as some employees stayed home for fear of arrest. The raids may also have affected the traditionally conservative politics of those towns.

Wichita State University's IKE Lab found a significant jump in September voter registrations in counties where the ICE raids took place, researcher and professor Alexandra Middlewood said.

VOTER REGISTRATIONS RISE

Oscar Soto, a grocery store owner in Dodge City, was shocked when he began seeing social media reports of ICE agents flooding his town on September 22. He joined with a group of community organizers to take meals to families afraid to leave home or whose providers had been arrested.

He said what he saw that week as he volunteered inspired him to register to vote for the first time at the age of 39.

“What can I do to help make any difference at all?" he said he asked himself. "And the one thing I landed on was voting."

He said he planned to vote for the Democrat.

In the 2024 election, Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote, but an October 5 Reuters/Ipsos poll showed just 24% of Hispanic Americans now approve of Trump's performance in the White House. Hispanic voters made up more than 9% of Kansas voters in 2024, according to the Pew Research Center.

CAMPAIGNS TRADE ATTACKS

Marshall's campaign has criticized Hamilton over an incident in which a volunteer at a camp connected to his church was accused of molesting two teenage boys. Church leaders initially only investigated the incident internally, later reporting it to police when the volunteer returned to the camp and was again accused of inappropriate behavior.

Hamilton has since said the church should have gone to police first and that it changed its policy after the incident to require that.

Hamilton’s campaign, in turn, has highlighted a September New York Times report that Marshall, an obstetrician before entering politics, sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical bills. Marshall said he had followed typical collection practices.

Marshall’s campaign did not respond to a request for an interview but issued a statement that said in part he had delivered for farmers, cut middle-class taxes and secured the border, and sought to tie Hamilton to national Democrats, calling him a “Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat,” referring to the Senate minority leader from New York.

In Garden City on October 9, a group of voters awaited Hamilton’s visit in a small café, including Michael Shull, a retired pediatrician and registered Republican.

Shull said he supported Hamilton because of his moderate political stances and because “he’s willing to talk to people.”

Speaking to Reuters after the event, Hamilton zeroed in on the message sent by voters like Shull in reliably Republican Kansas.

“It’s not just that Kansas is in play, and we might flip a seat,” Hamilton said. “It’s that people in a reliably red state are saying what’s happening in Washington, DC, is not OK.”

items.title: Explainer: What you need to know about the 2026 US midterm elections
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, October 21 - (This Oct. 19 story has been corrected to say 36 governors, not 39, in paragraph 25.)

Early voting has been underway for weeks ahead of the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, when US voters will elect members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country.

Held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, the midterms by definition do not involve the president. But for anyone who thinks they lack drama or importance this year, consider these two statistics:

More than 100 million people likely will cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022; and as of October 12, a record $3.8 billion had been spent on political advertisements that have been aired so far. Top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan, according to AdImpact, which tracks the activities.

Elon Musk alone has spent about $366 million to support Republicans, according to campaign finance records.

Still, midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races. More than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election, for example.

CONTROL OF CONGRESS AT STAKE

Plenty is at stake in this midterm election as Democrats try to win majority control of the US Congress.

Currently, Republicans hold a 218-214 majority in the House, where there are two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans. Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to win control.

Democrats also are fighting to win the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. They must net four additional seats to get control. Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.

CAN MIDTERMS AFFECT THE PRESIDENCY?

Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress. For 2026 that means that President Donald Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.

The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.

Midterm election results also can give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.

WHAT ARE POLLS SHOWING?

Approval of Trump's performance is at an all-time low of 32%, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to have an impact on the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.

At the same time, there is evidence that Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans. If early voting trends continue it could point to a Democratic win in November.

There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.

However, a landslide for the Democrats is far from assured. Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism towards Democrats, a Republican spending advantage on campaigns, and fears from moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.

RECENT MIDTERM HISTORY

Recent history tells the story of the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.

In the 2010 midterms, during the Democratic presidency of Barack Obama, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation. Democrats lost their majority. In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.

The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time. He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.

Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House. They gained a net total of 40 House seats, but lost a net two Senate seats.

This year's elections also have races for governors in 36 of the 50 states and voting in nearly every state for seats in their state-level legislative bodies.

Currently, Republicans control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.

WHO WILL BE SPEAKER?

If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York. He is currently the House Democratic leader.

Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to launch investigations into a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates. Jeffries repeatedly has said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.

Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House. He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.

A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job. Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."

MARQUEE RACES

Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign and an open seat in a Nebraska swing district where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran.

Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.

Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.

Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence. State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.

items.title: Trump drops threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier, citing US jobs
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON/MONTREAL, Oct 20 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump has dropped threats against Canadian jet maker Bombardier (BBDb.TO), opens new tab to ban it from the US market and instead vowed to take "good care" of the company's workers in Kansas.

Trump's threats in September against Bombardier became a political issue in Kansas, where it employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. The threatened ban prompted calls to the White House from Kansas lawmakers including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing a tough re-election bid.

"We're going to take care of Bombardier," Trump told 12 News in Kansas, citing Marshall's involvement.

At a speech Monday, Trump said he would help Bombardier.

"I'm going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away... I'll be helping them because I always viewed them as a Canadian company," Trump said. "But now I find out they have a presence here, and we're not hurting them if they're in Kansas. So we'll take care of those people and the jobs."

Bombardier's shares rose 4% Tuesday after Trump's comments. The White House declined to comment and referred questions to Trump's TV interview.

Bombardier, which in 1990 acquired Learjet and established its US headquarters in Kansas, has 3,500 jobs in the US, more than 40% of which are in Wichita.

Bombardier recently announced a North American Learning Center in Kansas and has said it workforce in the state is growing. Last week, it announced a $50 million investment in Wichita, where it has its defense headquarters, and also plans to open a facility in Fort Wayne, Indiana.

Last month, the Trump administration banned a broad swath of Canadian alcoholic beverages, motorcycles and dairy products from import, effective September 29, but took no action against Bombardier.

The action came after Canada's own retaliatory tariffs on US goods took effect in early September. Those were prompted after Washington imposed tariffs on some $20 billion of Canadian goods in August, after several rounds of negotiations collapsed.

Reuters reported last month it was not immediately clear how Trump could bar Bombardier private jets from being delivered to American customers since they have been approved by the US Federal Aviation Administration.

Threats by Trump in February to decertify Bombardier aircraft over a certification spat involving US rival Gulfstream Aerospace (GD.N), opens new tab never materialized, with regulator Transport Canada eventually approving the American-made jets.

items.title: Ahead of elections, Bessent says a Democrat-led Congress could do little to stop Trump agenda
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that there was not much a Democrat-led House of Representatives could do to stop the Trump administration's agenda.

"I think there's very little," Bessent said in an interview on 2Way TV two weeks ahead of November's midtermelections.

"We have very durable tariff authorities," he said, referring to Democrats' opposition to Trump broadly imposing tariffs on goods imported from countries around the world.

Control of Congress is at stake as voters head to the polls on November 3 to choose members of the House of Representatives and Senate and governors in states across the country. The Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The election comes as Trump's approval rating has dipped over his handling of the high cost of living for Americans during the US-Israeli war with Iran that has raised fuel prices.

Bessent said the Treasury's effort to isolate Iraneconomically was working.

"We haven't seen any loadings at the Iranian oil facility on Kharg Island since August. Iran currently has no oil on the water," he said.

"Panic is starting to set in ... I don't know whether it's going to take four more weeks or eight more weeks, but at a point, their economy will go nonlinear," he said.

Bessent also said he had not heard whether Russian President Vladimir Putin had accepted Trump's invitation to attend the G20 summit in Florida in December.

"I haven't seen his RSVP yea or nay yet," Bessent said.

Trump has said Russia has agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war in Ukraine.

items.title: Trump, Bloomberg ramp up spending ahead of midterms
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he would spend more than $400 million on Republican campaign efforts, while the New York Times reported that former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg was spending $80 million to help Democrats ahead of the November 3 midterm congressional elections.

The financial commitments come as Democrats seek to win control of Congress from Trump's Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.

"I have spent, or will be spending, over 400 Million Dollars by Election Day. More than 300 Million Dollars has already been spent on Advertising, Direct and Indirect Voter Contact, Rallies, Rally Arenas, Telerallies, Get Out the Vote Programs, Election Integrity, and more," Trump said in a social media post.

Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., and an affiliated group, No Going Back PAC, have spent at least $226 million on the elections so far, campaign filings show.

Bloomberg's team told the New York Times that he was sending about $80 million to Democrats in September and October.

Bloomberg's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The New York Times said at least $50 million of Bloomberg’s money was being used for House races, including $24 million for Everytown for Gun Safety, a group Bloomberg co-founded. He was also giving $16 million to House Majority PAC, the main super PAC aligned with House Democratic leadership.

Reuters has not independently verified the spending by Bloomberg.

items.title: USDA plans to resume imports of Mexican cattle at more ports of entry
items.content_html:
CHICAGO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - The US Department of Agriculture plans to resume cattle imports from Mexico at two additional US ports of entry, after halting shipments last year in an attempt to keep out the flesh-eating parasite New World screwworm, the agency said on Tuesday.

  • The USDA plans to restart imports in Columbus, New Mexico, on October 26 and, if conditions for safe trade are in place, in Nogales, Arizona, on November 30, according to a post on X.
  • The block on imports of Mexican cattle helped push US ground beef prices to record highs this year, contributing to rising concerns about food affordability ahead of midterm elections in November.
  • USDA resumed livestock trade in Douglas, Arizona, in August and at a large port in Santa Teresa, New Mexico, in September.
  • Horse imports are expected to resume in Santa Teresa on October 26, the USDA said on X.
  • The agency said it has confirmed 56 US screwworm cases since June, and 5 are active.

items.title: US to launch $8 billion support program for farmers to offset diesel costs, Trump says
items.content_html:
PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Monday the US Department of Agriculture will launch what he called a new "harvest fuel relief program" that will provide farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

"Tonight, I'm also pleased to announce that the Department of Agriculture will be launching a new harvest fuel relief program, providing our farmers with $8 billion in support to offset diesel costs during this harvest season," Trump said in a midterm election campaign speech in Kansas.

The announcement was the latest in a series of financial promises and pledges that the Republican leader has made to voters heading into the November midterm elections, where control of Congress is at stake.

The Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. However, Trump's approval rating has been low due to his handling of the high cost of living for Americans during the US-Israeli war on Iran that has raised fuel prices.

Trump and the Republican Party have been scrambling to maintain support in farm states with competitive Senate races as costs have risen.

Trump signed an executive order earlier this month that he said would expand access to tax-exempt diesel.

The Department of Agriculture said, opens new tab after Trump's speech on Monday that it would make $8 billion available "for one-time payments to American farmers this harvest season to provide relief during temporary market disruptions and increased input costs."

The program will provide what the department called "proportional support to producers using a uniform formula to cover a portion of modeled losses during the 2026 crop year."

The $8 billion in payments would be administered by the department's Farm Service Agency, the department said.

Trump has also separately proposed sending $5,000 checks to all adult citizens if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate in the midterms, though analysts, economists and even some Republicans in Congress have reacted with skepticism.

Earlier this month, Trump said the US government would send a one-time payment of $90 to more than 20 million Americans enrolled in Medicare, a health insurance program for the elderly.

items.title: US military weighs use of ‘mother of all bombs’ in potential future strikes on Iran, CNN says
items.content_html:
Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US military has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US officials familiar with the matter.

The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

Reuters could not immediately verify the report.

items.title: Trump warns Kansans that US will 'burn' like France if Democrats win
items.content_html:
PARK CITY, Kansas, Oct 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Monday used violent unrest in France as an argument against Democrats in his battle to defend a Kansas Senate seat long held by Republicans but in danger of falling to his political opponents.

Trump's rally on behalf of Republican incumbent Roger Marshall was his latest foray into conservative states where Republican candidates are on defense due to voter frustrations over the Iran war and rising prices.

"I love you Kansas, but I'm here for a guy named Roger Marshall," Trump said.

In a new addition to his stump speech, Trump pointed to widespread protests in France as a scenario that could erupt in the United States unless Republicans win. He provided no evidence.

France in recent days has seen some of the worst unrest in years as huge protests over the cost of living and underfunded public services descended into riots and looting.

Trump himself has struggled to make goods and services more affordable in the United States.

In his speech, Trump turned to anti-immigrant and anti-Muslim rhetoric, the type that he used to fuel his three presidential campaigns.

"We're not going to let that happen to this country," he said. "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America."

Trump has been mocking Democrats by calling them Dumocrats. Rights advocates have repeatedly criticized Trump for his rhetoric over the years in which he has targeted and mocked immigrants and ethnic minority groups. Civil rights groups say such rhetoric normalizes discriminatory attitudes towards those communities.

KANSAS COMPETITION

Kansas, a conservative Midwestern state Trump won by 16 points in 2024, has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 94 years. First-term Senator Marshall is in a close fight with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, pastor of a Methodist megachurch, who is running against Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president's “erratic leadership.”

“He wants you to repent for being born White,” Trump said of Hamilton.

Marshall, in remarks to the rally, led his campaign argument on cultural issues like stopping "radical Islam." He called Hamilton "too woke" for Kansas because he supports gay pride parades, which the crowd loudly booed.

"We need someone who can sort heifers and steers," he said.

In response, Hamilton's campaign spokesperson called Marshall's campaign "sinking."

"Nothing said at the rally can distract from the fact Kansans are being crushed by rising gas and diesel prices, struggling to access affordable healthcare, and are tired of Washington corruption," the spokesperson, Tyson Brody, said.

In a Monday video, Hamilton welcomed Trump to the state and said his supporters have “a place” in his campaign. Hamilton said he will work with Trump when it makes sense and stand up for Kansans when Washington policies hurt farmers and rural hospitals.

The tightness of the race is emblematic of the challenges looming for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections as they try to defy political headwinds and retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Trump is deep into a 32-day campaign blitz, frequently going to friendly areas that he won handily in previous elections.

One Republican familiar with Trump's midterm strategy said the president’s attention on rural parts of the country is in response to internal polling showing soft support from men 55 years and younger in rural areas nationwide, a voting bloc crucial to Trump’s 2024 presidential win.

ECONOMIC CONCERNS

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll, published on Monday, found that 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, a record low for the president.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

In Park City, near Wichita, many rallygoers walked more than a mile across Interstate 135 to reach the rural arena, as a red-and-green truck stop sign flashed its latest prices above their heads: $3.98 for gas and $5.78 for diesel.

That is up about 45% compared to average gas prices in the state last year, according to motoring club AAA.

Economic concerns were palpable among Trump's most loyal supporters.

“Being on disability, I don’t have much, but it seems like the prices are still going up and they need to come down. It feels like you’re having to search or hunt for food," said Monique Mullen, 59, a Republican voter from Hutchinson, Kansas, who takes care of her father.

A small bloc of protesters gathered near the arena, including James Nightingale, a self-described independent from Halstead, Kansas.

“I’m a farmer from Kansas and the Trump administration has decimated the farm economy in my area. Not only have his tariffs decimated our markets for grain sales, now he is bringing in imported beef from outside the country. What happened to ‘America First’?” he said.

Kansans have proven a willingness to cross parties, as voters have elected a Democratic governor, Laura Kelly, for the last two terms. "I don't think it's ever easy to get elected here," said Gina Seman, a Trump voter from Towanda, Kansas, noting that Republican candidates in the past have taken their popularity for granted.
